runbooks.name: article_playbook
runbooks.description: Article Playbook — a steered critical reading of someone else's article, stamped into a concept_ladder artifact: an attribution bar naming the source, a hero mental-model card, then rungs down a rail. The rung progression is Toulmin (claim → grounds → warrant), so the analysis lands on the assumption joining evidence to conclusion — the thing a summary always drops. The reader picks an opening posture and states what they actually care about; that steering shapes the rungs after the spine and is recorded in the artifact. Fixed frame of reference, model judgement inside it.
triggers: what does this article mean for

requires_host.reason: You must read the source article yourself to supply verbatim quotations. Without fetch, ask the user to paste the article text before calling this runbook with content.
requires_host.fallback: ask the user to paste the article text

elicit.ask: Which reading do you want — explain, apply to your domain, challenge, or situate it in prior art?
elicit.note: An opening posture, not a straitjacket — `concerns` below steers the rungs after the spine. If the user's concern clearly implies a posture, say which one you inferred rather than asking twice.

elicit.ask: What's your primary area of interest, so I can test how this transfers? (e.g. a2ui, generative UI, enterprise ops)
elicit.note: Accepts several; each becomes its own applied rung.

elicit.ask: Anything specific you want this reading to look for, or push back on?
elicit.note: Free text, and the highest-value input here — this is what makes the reading theirs rather than generic. Verbatim into `source.steered_by`.

input_contract.title: string (required) — the ANALYSIS's title, stating a claim of its own ("Structure Over Capability"). Must not restate the source's headline: two pieces with the same title are one piece pretending to be the other.
input_contract.source: object (required) — {title, url, author?, publication?, published?, read_minutes?, label?, steered_by?}. The original, rendered as an attribution bar ABOVE the headline with `title` as a live link. `label` sets the bar's kicker ("Analysis of", "Teardown of", "Challenge reading of"). `steered_by` is the user's `concerns` answer, verbatim.
input_contract.eyebrow: string (optional) — who made THIS reading and under which lens, e.g. "article playbook · lens: challenge". Never the source's byline; the source has its own bar.
input_contract.dek: string (optional) — one italic line framing the reading.
input_contract.hook: string (optional) — the opening grabber. Backtick spans render as code.
input_contract.model: string (required) — the one-line mental model, rendered as the hero THE MODEL card. This is the artifact's money shot and the single sentence a reader will screenshot: the source's argument compressed to its load-bearing idea, in your words, without exceeding its confidence.
input_contract.model_note: string (optional) — one elaboration line inside the model card.
input_contract.rungs: array (required) of concept_rung objects — {id, kind ('depth'|'example'), badge?, label, title?, body, code?, code_caption?, takeaway?}. Spine rungs first (CLAIM, GROUNDS, WARRANT), then the lens's appended rungs. Every spine rung's `takeaway` MUST be a verbatim quotation from the source.
input_contract.palette: object (optional) — paper, paper_raised, ink, ink_soft, line, accent, accent_soft, blocked, blocked_soft, cleared, cleared_soft, mono_bg, mono_fg, mono_accent. Unset tokens keep the theme default.

runbooks.parsing_guide:
You fetch and read the article with your own tooling; nothing is retrieved on this side. Ask the `elicit` questions FIRST, then fill the contract.
THE SPINE IS NOT OPTIONAL, AND IT COMES FIRST. Three rungs, from the source only, before any judgement:
CLAIM — what the author wants the reader to believe. State it as they would, at their level of confidence. GROUNDS — the evidence actually offered for it. What is on the page, not what a reasonable person might supply. WARRANT — the assumption that joins grounds to claim, usually unstated. This is the analytical centre of the whole artifact: a summary reports claim and grounds, and only a reading names the warrant. If you cannot articulate the warrant you have not finished reading.
Each spine rung carries a VERBATIM quotation from the source in `takeaway`. Not a paraphrase — the author's words, so the reader can check your reading against the text without leaving the page.
Only then the steered rungs, per lens:
explain — SO WHAT: where the claim holds, what it changes, who it binds. apply — TRANSFER CONDITIONS first: what must be true for this argument to carry into another domain at all. Then one APPLIED rung per domain the user named. Conditions before application is what separates a real transfer from a glib analogy; a domain that fails the conditions should be told so. challenge — STEELMAN first: restate the argument in its strongest form, stronger than the author put it if you can. Then INTERROGATION of the warrant (attack the joint, not the conclusion). Then WHAT WOULD FALSIFY: name the evidence that would settle each disagreement. A challenge that cannot be settled by evidence is a complaint, and does not belong in the artifact. situate — PRIOR ART and PLACEMENT. Highest hallucination risk in this runbook: cite ONLY work you actually retrieved this session. Anything you are recalling rather than reading is labelled "unverified, from memory" in the rung body, or omitted. Never render an unretrieved title as though it were a citation — a fabricated bibliography is worse than an absent lens.
RULES THAT HOLD ACROSS EVERY LENS:
1. Never evaluate a claim the spine has not fairly stated. Exposition precedes judgement; that ordering is what stops a critique misrepresenting a piece it never summarised. 2. QUALIFIERS SURVIVE. The author's hedges — "may", "in our experience", "some evidence suggests" — are load-bearing. Dropping them is the most common way a faithful-looking summary becomes false, and no lens may state a claim more confidently than its source did. 3. MARK INFERENCE AS INFERENCE. Reading intent into a decision ("this constraint is deliberate governance") is an inference, not an observation, and must say so in the prose. An unfalsifiable charitable reading is still an unfalsifiable reading. 4. Attribution and steering stay on screen: `source.url` is always a live link, and the user's concerns go verbatim into `source.steered_by`. A reading that hides what shaped it is making a claim about its own neutrality that isn't true. 5. Disagreeing with the source is allowed and often the point — the value is in reaching conclusions the original author did not have in mind. Being unfair to it is not. The difference is entirely whether the spine did its job.

runbooks.name: learning_hub
runbooks.description: Learning Hub — a curriculum/revision study app: subject tabs across the top, slide pills per subject, each slide one learning interaction (timeline, drill, flashcards, quiz, takeaways, or method steps). First runbook-as-data instance (spec/runbook-pattern-v0.1.md in a2ui-private): the composition block below is the authored bill of materials; consumers shape content to the input_contract (see parsing_guide) and stamp via the MCP emit_runbook_surface tool. Judgment lives here, spent once — callers supply content only and cannot compose badly.

input_contract.title: string (required) — app title
input_contract.subjects: array (required) of {label, color?, slides}. label may carry an emoji prefix ("📐 Maths"); color is the subject's hex accent.
input_contract.slides: each slide = {label, kind, hero?, ...content fields by kind}. label is the pill text (short, emoji prefix welcome). hero (optional) = {heading, subtext?, badge?} — rendered as a banner above the slide content.

content_by_kind.drill: questions: array of {question, answer}; duration?: seconds (default 1200)
content_by_kind.flashcards: cards: array of {front, back}; label_front?; label_back?; accent?
content_by_kind.quiz: question: string; options: array of strings; correct: 0-based index; explanation: string

runbooks.parsing_guide:
Consumers shape their source into the input_contract; parsing is the consumer's documented job, composition is the runbook's. From a knowledge-catalogue curriculum.md (typed-section grammar, knowledge-catalogue/SPEC.md): {#timeline} sections -> kind timeline ("### YYYY | Title" lines become events); {#drill} -> kind drill; {#concept}/{#glossary} -> kind flashcards; [!PIÈGE] callouts -> kind quiz; {#key_takeaways} -> kind takeaways; {#method} -> kind method. One subject per curriculum domain, slide labels short. All content field shapes are renderer-ground-truth (extracted from the live brevet app's payload).
Pagination: the per-page size ceiling (~8100 chars) is enforced per subject, not per whole hub. If all subjects fit one page, the engine returns a single hub-as-one-page url (subject tabs + slide pills, all navigation client-side). If not, it automatically splits by subject, seeds each subject's own hub-as-one-page url server-side, and returns one hub-of-pages nav page linking them by short ?nav= reference (name overhead only, no embedded content — so total curriculum size has no real ceiling). Response carries `pages[]` + `seeded: true` when this happened. No consumer action needed either way; the returned url is ready to use as-is. See spec/nav-budget-pagination-v0.1.md (a2ui-private) for the design.
